name: IRR
description: IRR (Internal Rate of Return) calculates the annualized percentage return of an investment based on a series of regular cash flows. It's the rate at which the net present value of all cash flows equals zero.
tldr: IRR tells you the annual return rate of an investment given its cash flows (initial cost + periodic returns). If IRR exceeds your required return, the investment is worthwhile.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: An array or range of cash flows. Must include at least one negative value (investment/cost) and one positive value (return/income).

parameters.name: guess
parameters.description: An estimated starting value for the iterative calculation. Default is 0.1 (10%). Usually unnecessary.

basicExample.description: Calculate the annual return rate of a $100,000 investment that returns $25,000 each year for 5 years
basicExample.explanation: The initial investment of -$100,000 (negative = cost) and 5 years of $25,000 returns (positive = income) yield an IRR of ~7.94%.

advancedExamples.title: Real estate investment IRR
advancedExamples.description: Evaluate a property purchase with varying annual rental income and a final sale
advancedExamples.explanation: B2:B8 contains: -$500K (purchase), $30K, $32K, $35K, $38K, $40K (rental income), $650K (sale price + final rent). IRR is 12.3%.

advancedExamples.title: IRR with irregular cash flows
advancedExamples.description: Calculate return for an investment with highly variable yearly returns
advancedExamples.explanation: Year 1 has no return, years 2-5 have increasing returns. IRR still computes the annualized rate that makes NPV=0.

advancedExamples.title: Compare IRR vs required return
advancedExamples.description: Use IF to compare IRR against a hurdle rate for investment decisions
advancedExamples.explanation: C1 contains the required minimum return (hurdle rate). If IRR exceeds it, the investment meets the threshold.

howItWorks: IRR uses an iterative algorithm to find the discount rate that makes the Net Present Value (NPV) of all cash flows exactly zero. Think of it this way: if you discount every future cash flow back to today at the IRR rate, the total exactly equals your initial investment. The calculation starts with the guess value (default 10%) and iteratively adjusts until NPV ≈ 0. Cash flows must be equally spaced in time (annual, monthly, etc.) and include at least one negative (cost) and one positive (return) value.

howToSteps.name: List all cash flows
howToSteps.text: Arrange cash flows in chronological order: initial investment (negative), then each period's return (positive or negative).

howToSteps.name: Enter values in cells
howToSteps.text: Put the cash flows in a column: B1 = initial cost (-$100K), B2-B6 = yearly returns ($25K each).

howToSteps.name: Calculate IRR
howToSteps.text: Type =IRR(B1:B6) to get the annualized return rate.

howToSteps.name: Compare to hurdle rate
howToSteps.text: If IRR > your required return, the investment is worth making.

limitations: IRR assumes equally-spaced time periods. For irregular timing, use XIRR instead.
IRR can produce multiple valid rates if cash flows change sign more than once (non-conventional cash flows).
IRR doesn't account for the scale of the investment — a 50% IRR on $1K is different from 50% on $1M.
The iterative calculation may fail to converge if the guess is far from the actual rate.

commonErrors.cause: IRR cannot find a solution after 20 iterations, or values contain no negative/positive numbers
commonErrors.fix: Provide a guess closer to the expected rate, or ensure values include at least one negative and one positive value.

commonErrors.cause: Cash flows change sign more than once (e.g., cost, profit, then cost again)
commonErrors.fix: For non-conventional cash flows, use MIRR (Modified IRR) which gives a single, meaningful rate.

commonErrors.cause: IRR ignores investment scale and reinvestment rate assumptions
commonErrors.fix: Use NPV alongside IRR for better decision-making. NPV accounts for scale and is more reliable.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: IRR works identically in Google Sheets with the same syntax and behavior.
googleSheetsEquivalent.notes: Google Sheets also supports XIRR for irregular-timed cash flows and MIRR for modified rate calculations.

faq.question: What's the difference between IRR and NPV?
faq.answer: NPV tells you the dollar value of an investment at a given discount rate. IRR tells you the discount rate that makes NPV=0. Use both: IRR for rate comparison, NPV for absolute value.

faq.question: When should I use XIRR instead of IRR?
faq.answer: Use XIRR when cash flows happen at irregular dates (not evenly spaced). XIRR takes specific dates for each cash flow, while IRR assumes equal time periods.

faq.question: What is MIRR and when should I use it?
faq.answer: MIRR (Modified IRR) fixes IRR's unrealistic reinvestment assumption. It assumes reinvestment at your finance rate and return at your reinvestment rate, giving a single, more realistic result.

faq.question: Why is IRR returning #NUM!?
faq.answer: Most common causes: (1) no negative values in the range (no initial cost), (2) no positive values (no returns), (3) the algorithm can't converge. Try providing a guess value.

faq.question: Is a higher IRR always better?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. A 100% IRR on a $100 investment earns less than a 20% IRR on a $1M investment. Always compare IRR alongside NPV for informed decisions.
